title: Wardrobe and Weather
premise: Petra Thornbury has spent a decade writing postcards to the family house on Larch Street, an address that burned down years ago, mailing them to no one and keeping carbon copies in a shoebox as proof of everything unsaid. When the surviving childhood home of their late aunt goes up for auction, Petra returns to town and finds the family's careful architecture of silence—built around the question of what happened the night of the fire—beginning to collapse. Sorting through the estate's wardrobe, where every garment carries a memory, Petra uncovers evidence that the fire was set deliberately by someone they've been protecting all along. In the end, with demolition scheduled for the lot, Petra finally asks the question aloud at a family gathering, shattering the arrangement but freeing everyone to speak; the book closes with Petra writing one last postcard—addressed, for the first time, to a living person.
about_author: Freya Vasquez is a former archivist who spent years cataloguing other people's letters before turning to fiction about the things families refuse to say. She writes from a small coastal town where she keeps her own collection of unsent correspondence.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Petra, in third-person limited POV, sorts their shoebox of carbon-copied postcards addressed to the burned house on Larch Street. We learn the ritual: one postcard a week, ten years running. The emotional beat is quiet compulsion—the sense that this habit is both armor and wound.

chapters.title: Auction Notice
chapters.summary: Petra receives a legal notice: Aunt Marguerite's house—the last intact family property—is going to auction, with demolition of the Larch Street lot scheduled the same month. Petra's sister Dree calls, breezy and deflecting. The beat is dread disguised as logistics.

chapters.title: What the Fire Took
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, still Petra's POV: the night of the fire twenty-two years ago, rendered in fragments. Someone was in the kitchen; someone left through the garden door. The family never spoke of it again. The beat is the vertigo of half-memory.

chapters.title: Return to Town
chapters.summary: Petra drives back to their hometown, checks into a motel, and walks past the empty Larch Street lot, now weeds and chain-link. A neighbor recognizes them and says too warmly, 'You look just like her.' The beat is the shock of being seen after years of chosen invisibility.

chapters.title: The Estate Sale Preview
chapters.summary: At the preview auction, Petra wanders Marguerite's rooms and finds the wardrobe: decades of clothes, each tagged with handwritten labels in Marguerite's script. Cousin Theo appears, friendly but watchful. The beat is tenderness laced with suspicion—who else wants the house emptied fast?

chapters.title: Dree's Version
chapters.summary: Over diner coffee, Dree offers her polished account of the family: happy, ordinary, tragic only by accident. Petra notices how rehearsed it sounds. The beat is the friction between love and narrative—sisters who can't share a version of the truth.

chapters.title: Labels
chapters.summary: Petra begins reading the wardrobe tags closely: 'worn the night of the storm,' 'burnt sleeve, kept anyway.' One dress is labeled with a date—the fire's date—and smells faintly of smoke. The beat is dawning realization that Marguerite was keeping records too.

chapters.title: Theo's Offer
chapters.summary: Theo proposes pooling money so the family buys the house together and 'keeps things simple.' His eagerness reads as generosity or containment. Petra declines to commit. The beat is the pressure of being recruited into silence.

chapters.title: Postcard Interrupted
chapters.summary: Petra tries to write the week's postcard and cannot finish it; the ritual breaks for the first time in ten years. In its place, they write a list of questions they've never asked anyone. The beat is the armor cracking from inside.

chapters.title: The Garden Door
chapters.summary: Investigating the old house, Petra finds the garden door hinge freshly oiled and a key hidden above the frame—someone has been entering. Footprints in the cellar dust. The beat is fear sharpening into purpose: the past isn't past; it's active.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Letters
chapters.summary: In the attic, Petra discovers a bundle of letters Marguerite wrote to their mother—unmailed—rehearsing the same question over and over: 'Tell me what you saw.' The beat is grief and kinship across generations of people circling the same unsaid thing.

chapters.title: Mother's Silence
chapters.summary: Petra visits their mother, Vivian, in her assisted-living apartment. Vivian is lucid, charming, and absolutely sealed. When Petra mentions the fire, she changes the subject to weather—an echo of the title. The beat is loving someone who chooses the wall.

chapters.title: The Auction
chapters.summary: The auction itself: strangers buy the furniture, the piano, the life. Petra bids on and wins only the wardrobe, hauling it to the motel room like a body. The beat is bereavement—the material self of a family dispersed to the highest bidders.

chapters.title: Smoke in the Seams
chapters.summary: Going through the wardrobe properly, Petra finds sewn into a coat lining a photograph and a train ticket dated the day after the fire—in Theo's father's name. The beat is betrayal arriving quietly, folded in wool.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Lot
chapters.summary: Petra confronts Theo at the Larch Street lot. He admits his father set the fire—to cover debts—and that the family arranged its silence around protecting him, then him. The beat is fury and pity tangled; the question forming in Petra's throat.

chapters.title: Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: The demolition date moves up: five days. Theo begs Petra to let it go now that the house will be rubble anyway. Dree sides with him, terrified. The beat is the closing window—speak now or be buried with the lot.

chapters.title: Vivian's Door
chapters.summary: Petra shows their mother the photograph. For the first time, Vivian stops performing; she admits she knew, and that her silence was the price of keeping the family whole. 'You don't ask,' she says, 'because the answer rearranges everyone.' The beat is the wall becoming a door.

chapters.title: The Question
chapters.summary: Climax: at an improvised family dinner, with the demolition two days away, Petra stands and asks the question the family arranged itself around: 'Who set the fire, and why did we all agree not to know?' The room fractures—denial, weeping, Dree walking out, Theo finally saying his father's name aloud. The beat is rupture as liberation.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: The days after: Dree doesn't call, then does; Theo leaves town; Vivian sleeps for a day and wakes lighter. Petra sits with the wreckage of the family's old architecture and finds, beneath it, something livable. The beat is raw, unglamorous relief.

chapters.title: Rubble
chapters.summary: Petra watches the Larch Street lot demolished from across the street, holding the smoke-smelling dress. Neighbors gather silently beside them. The beat is mourning that no longer requires secrecy—grief performed in public, together.

chapters.title: One Last Postcard
chapters.summary: Petra writes a final postcard—but addresses it to Dree, alive and reachable, describing the weather and nothing else. It's enough. The shoebox is retired to a shelf, not thrown away. The beat is the transformation of ritual from hiding to reaching.

chapters.title: Wardrobe and Weather
chapters.summary: Epilogue months later: Petra hangs Marguerite's labeled garments in their own closet, each tag now a small archive of a survived past. A postcard arrives from Dree—weather, a joke, a question about next summer. The beat is inheritance redefined: not silence passed down, but the courage to ask.
